name: Yusuf Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. How does a normal working day go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenfield Hyper, the huge supermarket on the retail park off the bypass. Mostly I'm on the tills, but I'm the senior on garden and electronics too, so I'm the one they call when a customer wants a lawnmower explained. It's fine. You get your head down, do it well and go home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being good at it. I can scan a trolley in my sleep and I know where everything is in a store the size of two football pitches. What grinds me is the walking, the car park wind in the winter and customers who treat you like part of the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I think, which is that it's a lot of noise. We've had self-scanners for years, and the checkout is still full of people. I'd say fine, whatever, let's see it work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I don't think much about it. I'm thinking about the rent on our flat, the car payment and whether Kelly's salon will hold steady. We've got maybe two weeks of savings if both of us stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. Work, watch the football, pay what's due. I'd probably pick up a few more Saturday shifts, since there's usually somebody sick. I'd skip the holiday we talk about every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. It's more of a shrug. When nothing changes you don't have to think, and I'm okay with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you keep your head down. How do you feel about talk of AI at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday first, then the takeaways. Kelly would say cut my gaming subscription, and she'd be right. The car I'd never sell because I need it for the retail park, and there's no bus out there at 6am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't blame anyone. Business is business, and a hypermarket has to keep costs down. If wages don't keep up, I'd think about asking for a rise, but I'd be nervous to do it.

say: AI is a lot of **noise**, and we've had self-scanners for years with the checkout still full.
think: I don't think much about AI, more about **rent**, the car payment and Kelly's salon.
We have about **two weeks** of savings if both stop earning.
do: Pick up extra **Saturday shifts** when someone's sick.
Cancel the gaming subscription and cut **takeaways**.
feel: A **shrug**: when nothing changes you don't have to think.
S0.quote: When nothing changes you don't have to think, and I'm okay with that.
fieldNote: Gives AI very little **attention**, yet money pressure is constant.
Avoids blame and conflict, and is **nervous** about asking for a rise.
The car is non-negotiable because there's no **bus** to the retail park at 6am.

steps.text: Pick up extra Saturday shifts when someone calls in sick
Skip the holiday and cancel the gaming subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the shop will cut office people before tills, because the tills are still a person job when something breaks. I've seen the till system get smarter every year, and the queue's still there. Friends would hear me say it's coming, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it makes me edgy. Ordering and planning are the head office parts, but I'm the senior on garden and electronics, and if they put an AI chat on the website, customers might not ask me anything. Then I'm just a till and a trolley collector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and ask my manager what's coming, so I'm not caught out. I'd do the training they give, but I won't be the first to try anything. I'd put 40 a month away, which means giving up my gym day passes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a notch up from the first one. It's the feeling of a rumour going round the break room, and you don't know if it's about you. I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks around you would software take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they brought in a system that tells us when to restock. Two weeks later, Dev (a colleague) got moved off the stock team and nobody told him why. I remember thinking, if they do that to him, they'll do it to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new tools if the shop asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let me be careful: I'd ask for it in writing. Nobody should be moved or cut without notice, and the senior staff should get a say. That's reasonable. I wouldn't want to be called difficult, though.

say: The shop will cut **office** people before tills, because tills still need a person when something breaks.
think: If an AI chat answers customers about garden and electronics, I'm just a **till** and a trolley collector.
It makes me **edgy**, like a rumour in the break room.
do: Ask my manager what's **coming** so I'm not caught out.
Do the **training** they give but not be first to try anything.
Put **40 a month** away by dropping gym day passes.
feel: **Uneasy**, not knowing whether the rumour is about me.
S1.quote: Nobody should be moved or cut without notice, and the senior staff should get a say.
fieldNote: Reads change through **rumour** and colleagues' fates, not through technology.
Wants **notice in writing** but fears being called difficult.
Mood rises because his **specialist** role could be bypassed.

steps.text: Ask the manager what systems are coming before changing anything
Do the shop's training on new tools without being first to try them
Put 40 a month aside by dropping gym day passes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing, honestly, because it'd cause a panic. To friends I'd say the government had better do something, because two years isn't long. I'd say it badly, probably, since I'm not a talker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared. Thinking AI takes the head-office jobs and the website first, then three years later robots in the shop. I'm 27 now, so by 2031 I'm 31 with a till skill and no other trade, and few jobs around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't needed, move in with Kelly's mum if rent went bad, and put every spare penny in the bank. I'd ask the job centre what courses are free, because I wouldn't know where to start. I'd say yes to every extra shift while the shop still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops when I picture it. I'm the sort who needs a plan, and I haven't got one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's two years. What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kelly's salon is a hands-on job, so she might be the one who has work longest. That's a strange thing to say, but she'd be the main earner and I'd be the one who retrains. I'd hate that, I think, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for Kelly and you together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather be the one who says what's on my mind. At the moment I put it in a drawer. If it came to it, I'd talk to Kelly the same night and not leave it a week.

say: Two years isn't long, so **government** had better do something.
I'd say it badly, because I'm not a **talker**.
think: By 2031 I'm 31 with a **till skill** and no other trade, and few jobs around here.
Thinking AI takes head-office jobs first and **robots** follow three years later.
do: Stop all spending that isn't **needed** and save every spare penny.
Ask the **job centre** which courses are free.
Move in with Kelly's **mum** if rent goes bad.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a dropping stomach and no plan.
S2.quote: My stomach drops when I picture it. I'm the sort who needs a plan, and I haven't got one.
fieldNote: Hides his fear at **work** and shows it only in private.
Accepts a role where **Kelly** is the main earner, with discomfort.
Doesn't know how to **retrain**, so the first step is asking the job centre.

steps.text: Stop all spending that isn't needed and save every spare penny
Ask the job centre which retraining courses are free
Move in with Kelly's mum if the rent gets out of reach
Say yes to every extra shift while the shop needs me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time, but only if somebody tells us what to do. At work I'd keep my head down and ask a few questions. Friends would hear me say the government and the shop should team up on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's still a worry, but I'd feel I have a bit of room. 2031 is when thinking AI is everywhere, and 2034 when robots reach the tills. I'd be 32, and I think I could do a course by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the local college for something practical, maybe a forklift licence or a warehouse supervisor certificate, and take it part-time. I'd save 100 a month and not buy a new car. I'd keep the job and the Saturday shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. I'd still be anxious that I'd leave it too late, since I'm good at putting things off. If someone put a date in my calendar, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, do you get busier or just wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person to tell me which course is real. There are lots of adverts for courses, and I don't trust half of them. A name at the shop or the council would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What helps you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a mate doing it alongside me. If Dev and I both went to the same evening class, I'd turn up. I'm not good at it alone.

say: Five years is enough time, but only if somebody tells us **what to do**.
The government and the shop should team up on **training**.
think: It's still a worry, but I'd have a bit of **room** before 2034.
I'd be **32**, and I think I could do a course by then.
do: Look at a practical **college** course, such as a forklift licence or warehouse supervisor certificate.
Save **100 a month** and keep the old car.
Keep the job and the **Saturday** shifts.
feel: **Worried** but not frozen, afraid of leaving it too late.
S3.quote: There are lots of adverts for courses, and I don't trust half of them.
fieldNote: The extra time helps him only if **guidance** and a study partner exist.
Self-aware about **procrastination** and relies on dates and people.
Picks **warehouse** work, a hands-on path that sits behind the robot date.

steps.text: Enrol part-time in a forklift licence or warehouse supervisor course
Save 100 a month and keep the old car
Keep the shop job and the Saturday shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's plenty of time, so let's not panic. I'd say it with a joke. At the pub I'd say the government has ten years to sort it out and they'd better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly okay. By 2036 I'm 37, and 2039 for the robots I'd be 40. That's a lot of time to find another line of work, as long as I don't do the usual and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and slowly build a plan: a course in the next year or two, some savings, and a better job by about 2032. I'd also try to get a flat deposit together if I could, though it feels far off. I'd probably still not use AI at work until forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A long runway is a relief, because I can get on with life and not live in dread. The worry is still there at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do anything differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd treat it as a long way off and forget about it. A deadline in ten years is like a gym membership in January. I'd need Kelly to nag me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong with having so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say save first, because money is what makes choices possible. Learn a trade, even a small one. And don't pretend it won't affect you because you're not in an office.

say: Ten years is plenty of time, so **don't panic**, but government had better sort it out.
think: I feel mostly okay, as long as I don't do the usual and **leave it**.
do: Build a slow **plan**: a course in a year or two, and a better job by about 2032.
Try to put together a **flat deposit**.
Still avoid **AI** at work until forced to.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with the worry at the back.
S4.quote: A deadline in ten years is like a gym membership in January. I'd need Kelly to nag me.
fieldNote: Calmer, but thin savings and **inertia** keep him anxious rather than uneasy.
Honest about his habit of **delay**, and relies on Kelly.
Still the least **tech-curious** of his group.

steps.text: Start a practical trade course within the next two years
Build savings toward a flat deposit
Aim for a better-paid job by about 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. There's no time to retrain, and I've no savings to cover it. What would help is free courses, some money to live on while I do one, and an employer who tells us the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Just that people like me aren't stupid, we just don't shout. A lot of us are quietly worried and don't know who to ask.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't stupid, we just don't shout. A lot of us are quietly worried and don't know who to ask.
portrait: Yusuf is 27, a **senior** till operator and the garden and electronics go-to at a huge retail-park supermarket.
He lives with Kelly (his partner), a hairdresser, and has about **two weeks** of savings with few jobs nearby.
He never uses AI, hides his worry at work and blames **no one**, saying business is business.
He moves from a shrug in the quiet scenario to **alarm** in 2028, with no plan and no idea where to start.
His best fix would be a **study partner**, a trusted guide to real courses, and some living money.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there is no time to retrain and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses**, living money while he studies, and an employer who tells the truth early.
